India's approach to orbital safety

India's increasing involvement in satellite operations makes the protection of the orbital environment important for government missions and private activities alike. Safe operation requires observing objects in space, assessing collision risks, exchanging useful information and disposing of spacecraft responsibly.

Several Indian initiatives contribute to these objectives. Their names are similar in purpose, but their functions are not identical.

NETRA: Tracking and analysis of space objects

NETRA stands for Network for Space Objects Tracking and Analysis. It is an ISRO initiative to improve India's ability to observe and analyse objects in space, including potential debris hazards.

Its planned and developing capabilities involve observational infrastructure such as radars and optical telescopes, together with facilities for processing tracking information and assessing close approaches.

The ISRO Space Situational Awareness Control Centre associated with NETRA was inaugurated on 14 December 2020 at the ISTRAC campus in Peenya, Bengaluru.

NETRA therefore relates primarily to obtaining and analysing information about the orbital environment. It should not be confused with an agency responsible for authorising private space activities.

IS4OM: Coordination of safe and sustainable operations

IS4OM stands for ISRO System for Safe and Sustainable Space Operations Management. Dedicated in 2022, it coordinates ISRO's efforts related to space situational awareness, collision-risk assessment, reentry monitoring and the safety and sustainability of space operations.

NETRA and IS4OM are related but distinct. NETRA concerns the tracking-and-analysis network and its supporting facilities; IS4OM has a broader coordination role in managing safe and sustainable operations.

Debris-Free Space Missions: India's 2030 objective

India announced its Debris-Free Space Missions (DFSM) initiative on 16 April 2024 during the 42nd annual meeting of the Inter-Agency Space Debris Coordination Committee in Bengaluru.

The initiative aims for debris-free missions by 2030 across Indian space actors, including government organisations and private entities. The objective involves preventing unnecessary debris, avoiding collisions and break-ups, and ensuring proper end-of-mission disposal.

IS4OM serves as a nodal point for implementing the initiative with support from other relevant institutions. The initiative represents a target and programme of action; it does not establish that every Indian mission was already debris-free when the initiative was announced.

Status at 4 November 2026: DFSM's 2030 goal remains a future objective. India's annual space-situational reports describe ongoing tracking, assessment and debris-reduction activities rather than a completed elimination of orbital debris.

What India's latest completed-year assessment shows

The Indian Space Situational Awareness Report for 2025 covers the calendar year from 1 January to 31 December 2025. ISRO released its summary on 16 April 2026.

The report described approximately 160,000 close-approach alerts during 2025, illustrating the burden of monitoring an increasingly crowded orbital environment. These were alerts concerning possible close approaches, not 160,000 actual collisions.

The report also recorded an Indian example of end-of-mission disposal. In 2025, the IRNSS-1D navigation satellite was moved to a graveyard orbit nearly 600 km above the geostationary region and passivated. The spacecraft had operated in an inclined geosynchronous orbit. Its disposal illustrates how a retired satellite can be moved away from a heavily used orbital region.

These details belong to the report's 2025 data period and should not be interpreted as real-time counts or the status of every spacecraft in November 2026.

Gujarat's connection to India's space sector

Ahmedabad, Gujarat, hosts important institutions involved in space technology, research and the participation of non-governmental entities. These institutions have different functions.

InstitutionLocationMain connection
Space Applications Centre (SAC)Ahmedabad, GujaratISRO centre developing space applications and payload technologies for fields such as communication, navigation and remote sensing.
IN-SPACeAhmedabad, GujaratPromotes, enables and authorises space activities, including private participation.
Physical Research Laboratory (PRL)Ahmedabad, GujaratScientific research in areas including space, planetary and atmospheric sciences; an autonomous institution under DOS.
NETRA SSA Control CentreBengaluru, KarnatakaSupports space-object tracking information, analysis and close-approach assessment.

Space Applications Centre

The Space Applications Centre (SAC) is an ISRO centre in Ahmedabad. Its work contributes to the development of spaceborne systems and applications useful for communication, remote sensing and navigation. For example, Earth-observation capabilities can help provide information used in agriculture, water-resource assessment and disaster management.

IN-SPACe and Physical Research Laboratory

IN-SPACe is also located in Ahmedabad, but its responsibilities differ from those of SAC. Its focus is promotion, enablement and authorisation of space activities. It is not simply another name for an ISRO satellite-development centre.

The Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) is a research institution in Ahmedabad associated with the Department of Space. Its scientific work must be distinguished from the authorisation functions of IN-SPACe and the commercial functions of NSIL.

Although Gujarat is important to India's space programme, NETRA's SSA Control Centre is in Bengaluru, not Ahmedabad. Institutional location and institutional function are separate facts and should both be learned accurately.

Connecting sustainability, governance and participation

Space sustainability involves 3 linked responsibilities. First, spacecraft operators should reduce debris and avoid unnecessary collision risks. Second, international principles establish peaceful-use obligations, state responsibility and liability for damage. Third, India's institutions and private participants must carry out their different functions within this shared framework.

A private satellite can provide a useful service, but it may also create collision risks if operated carelessly or abandoned in a crowded orbit. Technical safety measures, public oversight and international cooperation therefore support the same objective: keeping outer space usable for future missions.

Prelims focus

  • NETRA means Network for Space Objects Tracking and Analysis; its SSA Control Centre is in Bengaluru.
  • IS4OM coordinates efforts for safe and sustainable space operations.
  • DFSM was announced on 16 April 2024 and aims for debris-free Indian missions by 2030.
  • ISSAR-2025 covers calendar year 2025; its summary was released on 16 April 2026.
  • SAC, IN-SPACe and PRL are associated with Ahmedabad, Gujarat.
  • Trap: NETRA tracks and analyses orbital hazards, IN-SPACe enables and authorises space activities, and NSIL has a commercial role.

[Sources: ISRO, ISRO SSA Control Centre Inaugurated, 14 December 2020, section on the NETRA project and its control centre; ISRO, Indian Space Situational Assessment Report for 2022, released 3 April 2023, sections on IS4OM; ISRO, India's Intent on Debris-Free Space Missions – Explained, 19 April 2024, sections on the 2030 objective and implementation; ISRO, Indian Space Situational Awareness Report for 2025 Released, 16 April 2026, sections on close-approach alerts, Indian objects and debris-reduction efforts, data period 1 January–31 December 2025; ISRO, Department of Space Centres and Units, entries for SAC, IN-SPACe and PRL; ISRO, Space Applications Centre, institutional functions; Physical Research Laboratory, institutional research areas. Online institutional information accessed 4 November 2026.]

title: India's Space-Safety Initiatives and Gujarat's Space Institutions
